land.text: the eastern half of the Kushan realm: the Punjab, Taxila, the Doab and the Gangetic plain

predecessors.note: Kushan Empire page: 'After the death of Vasudeva I in 225, the Kushan empire split into western and eastern halves.' Cliopatria starts the half in 238; the page's year is 225, so the half starts here in 226.

land.text: the Punjab: 1,029 of the shape's 1,141 cells lie in Cliopatria's Gupta shape of 347

successors.note: Samudragupta subjugated the Eastern Kushans in the mid-4th century (Kushan Empire page); the Allahabad pillar has the Kushan rulers offering themselves and their daughters, and the Samudragupta page says the Kushans still ruled the Punjab 'under the suzerainty of the Gupta Emperor'. The Kushan line did not end: Kipunada (c. 335-350) is its last ruler on the list.

land.text: Peshawar and Gandhara, conquered by the Kidarites c. 390-410, who seem to have held central and western Punjab for some time afterward

successors.note: Kidarites page; Kidara styled himself 'Kidara King of the Kushans' and some Kidarites became a ruling dynasty of the Kushan Empire, hence 'Little Kushans'.

capitals.name: Taxila
capitals.note: The Kushan Empire page puts the Eastern Kushans in the Punjab with their capital at Taxila and its infobox gives Taxila for the 3rd-4th centuries; it adds that Vasudeva II ruled from Taxila as a 'Little Kushan'.

rulers.name: Kanishka II
rulers.note: 'c. 230-247'; Sanchi inscriptions of years 22 and 28 of a second Kanishka era. The page's list of later rulers does not say which half each ruled, and Vasudeva I appears to 230 on it (225 in the text), so 226-229 has no ruler here.

rulers.name: Vasudeva II
rulers.note: 'c. 270-300'; ruled from Taxila as a 'Little Kushan'.

rulers.name: Kipunada
rulers.note: 'c. 335-350', the last Kushan ruler on the page; Cliopatria's row ends in 346. Reviewer (sa-02-c): clipped to the dossier's end, 346.

correction.text: the 238 shape held 13 years earlier: the eastern half of the Kushan realm, based in the Punjab with its capital at Taxila

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria starts the Eastern Kushans in 238; the Kushan Empire page puts the split of the empire into western and eastern halves just after 225. The Kushan Empire row (to 237) is, to within 54 cells, the union of the two halves' 238 shapes, so the halves are drawn from 226 with the 238 outline. No infobox area exists for the divided state; the page's 2.0-2.5 M km2 (c. 200) is for the undivided empire, against 1.92 M km2 for the two halves together.

1.24 M km2: the Punjab, Sindh, Rajasthan, the Doab, Awadh, Uttar Pradesh and 130 cells of Gandhara. The Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom page has the Sasanians capturing 'Sogdia, Bactria and Gandhara' in 225 and Shapur I (240-270) reaching Purushapura (Peshawar), so Gandhara in this shape is doubtful from the start; the page also says almost none of the Kushano-Sasanian coinage has been found at Taxila, which fits a Kushan Punjab. Sindh, Rajasthan and Gujarat are not on any page opened for this state; the Western Satraps' Junagadh list of 150 names the same lands (see notes).

1.19 M km2: 188 cells of Gandhara (the Peshawar valley) pass to Cliopatria's Indo-Sasanian Empire of 260; the Kushano-Sasanian page puts the Sasanian advance 'further to the eastern parts of their empire in western Pakistan during the reign of his son Shapur I (240-270)' and says it 'apparently did not cross the Indus River', with Gandhara the farthest point. The year 260 is Cliopatria's.

0.31 M km2: the Gangetic plain, Rajasthan and Haryana and 1,339 cells of Sindh, Rajasthan and the southern Punjab are removed (the last to the Western Satraps, see their dossier). The Kushan Empire page: territories on the Gangetic plain became independent around 270, which agrees with the year. Only the Punjab, a strip of Gandhara and Kashmir remain, 46% Punjab.
Identical to 270 within 105 km2; no page dates a change in 283.

Identical to 283. Samudragupta's reign is c. 335-375 on his page; the Allahabad pillar claims the homage of the Daivaputra-Shahi-Shahanushahi, read as Kushan rulers by Eraly and others; 1,029 of the 1,141 cells lie in the Gupta shape of 347.

region.text: the Punjab, the Doab and the Gangetic plain, with Taxila

ledger.note: 226: the eastern half of the Kushan realm becomes the Eastern Kushans. 'After the death of Vasudeva I in 225, the Kushan empire split into western and eastern halves'; the eastern half was based in the Punjab with its capital at Taxila. The Vasudeva I dates differ on the page (died 225; list c. 190-230). Cliopatria begins the half in 238.

region.text: Gandhara up to Purushapura (Peshawar), where Shapur I claimed Kushan land to end

ledger.note: 240: Shapur I's Sasanians push east towards Gandhara. The Sasanians went 'further to the eastern parts of their empire in western Pakistan during the reign of his son Shapur I (240-270)' (Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom page); Shapur's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam claims Kushan territory 'as far as Purushapura' (Kushan Empire page). The first campaign is not dated; the reign's start is used.

region.text: the Peshawar valley (Gandhara), 184 of the 188 cells lost in 260

ledger.note: c. 260: the Peshawar valley passes to the Sasanian-ruled Kushano-Sasanians. The page gives Shapur I's reign (240-270) for the advance into western Pakistan and Gandhara as the farthest point; 260 is Cliopatria's year, when its Indo-Sasanian row begins.

region.text: Gandhara, the farthest eastern extent of the Kushano-Sasanians

ledger.note: 270: Shapur I's reign ends (240-270) with the Sasanians at the Indus; the page says they 'apparently did not cross the Indus River' and that coins of Sasanian type appear at Taxila only from Shapur II's reign.

region.text: the Gangetic plain (Doab, Awadh, Magadha, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar) and, beyond what the page names, Haryana and parts of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh

ledger.note: c. 270: the Gangetic plain becomes independent of the Kushans. The Kushan Empire page says the territories on the Gangetic plain became independent around 270 and lists the Nagas of Padmavati and of Vindhyatabi among the empire's successors; its words are 'Around 270 their territories on the Gangetic plain became independent under local dynasties such as the Yaudheyas' (Cliopatria's Yaudheya row begins only in 306, hence 'nobody'). Cliopatria's 270 loss is larger: it also strips Rajasthan and bits of Madhya Pradesh; Haryana is the Yaudheyas' country (Rudradaman page). The Nagas of Padmavati page: the Nagas 'rose to power after the decline of the Kushan Empire in north-central India, in the early 3rd century', there is 'no concrete evidence' that they defeated the Kushans, and the kingdom 'eventually expanded to include Mathura in north and Ujjain in south'; its last king Ganapati-naga fell to Samudragupta in the mid-4th century. So 'nobody' here stands for the local rulers and the Nagas, not for an empty land.

region.text: Sindh, southern Punjab and western Rajasthan: the 1,339 cells shared with the Western Satraps' 270 shape

ledger.note: c. 270: Sindh, the southern Punjab and western Rajasthan pass to the Western Satraps in Cliopatria. No page opened for this state mentions it; the Kushan Empire page lists the Western Satraps only among the empire's predecessors, and the Western Satraps pages (opened for another dossier) have Rudradaman holding Sindhu-Sauvira, Maru and Kukura already in 150.

region.text: the Punjab and the Peshawar fringe

ledger.note: c. 346: Samudragupta's Guptas absorb the Eastern Kushans' Punjab. The Kushan Empire page says Samudragupta subjugated the Eastern Kushans in the mid-4th century; the Allahabad pillar says the Kushan rulers offered 'self-surrender, offering (their own) daughters in marriage', and the Kushans kept their districts under his suzerainty (Samudragupta page). The page gives no year: 346 is Cliopatria's last year (Gupta shape of 347 holds 1,029 of the 1,141 cells); Kipunada's reign is listed c. 335-350 and Samudragupta's c. 335-375.

wars.name: Shapur I's eastern campaign against the Kushans
wars.outcome: The Sasanians took the Kushan provinces of Sogdia, Bactria and Gandhara and held them to the Indus; Shapur I's inscription claims Kushan territory as far as Purushapura.
wars.note: The page gives three dates: 225 for the capture, about 230 for Ardashir I's dominion in Bactria and 240-270 for Shapur I's advance into western Pakistan.

wars.name: Samudragupta's subjugation of the Kushans

zones.text: the Punjab, where the Kushans 'still ruled... under the suzerainty of the Gupta Emperor'

wars.outcome: The Kushan rulers sought the favour of Samudragupta, offering daughters in marriage and using the Garuda seal; they kept their districts as his subordinates.
wars.note: Years are Samudragupta's reign (c. 335-375); the page dates no conquest. The identification of the Daivaputra-Shahi-Shahanushahi with the Kushans is Eraly's and others'; Bakker reads Shahanushahi as Shapur II and Bhandarkar proposes one ruler, possibly Kidara I.

certainty.note: The Punjab frontier with the Sasanians at the Indus and the Gangetic breakaway of c. 270 are approximate; none is a treaty line.

sources.title: Kushan Empire
sources.note: The split after 225, the Eastern Kushans in the Punjab with Taxila as capital, the Gangetic breakaway c. 270, Samudragupta's mid-4th-century subjugation, the later rulers' list.

sources.title: Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom
sources.note: Sasanian capture (225), Shapur I (240-270) in western Pakistan, 'did not cross the Indus', coins at Taxila.

sources.title: Samudragupta
sources.note: Allahabad pillar passage on the Kushan rulers, the Punjab under Gupta suzerainty, reign c. 335-375.

sources.title: Kidarites
sources.note: The Kidarite conquest of Peshawar and Gandhara c. 390-410, 'Little Kushans', Kidara 'King of the Kushans'.

sources.title: Nagas of Padmavati
sources.note: The Nagas of Padmavati: rise in the early 3rd century after Kushan decline, no concrete evidence of a defeat of the Kushans, expansion to Mathura and Ujjain, end under Samudragupta.

notes:
Pages opened: five, the whole 5-page budget (Kushan Empire, Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom, Samudragupta, Kidarites, Nagas of Padmavati). The Kanishka, Kujula Kadphises, Vima Kadphises and the Satrap pages opened for sibling dossiers are not cited here.

One state or three: see the kushan-empire notes. Cliopatria's Eastern Kushans (238-346), Western Kushans (238-259) and Kushan Empire (43-237) share Wikidata Q25979. The pages treat the Kushans as one empire that divided after Vasudeva I's death in 225, so this dossier starts in 226 (a new keyframe takes the 238 outline back 12 years) and the empire's dossier ends in 225. The Eastern Kushans are the continuation of the Kushan dynasty (the Kushan Empire page lists Kanishka II to Kipunada among the later Kushan rulers), so the colour agent should keep them in the Kushan family.

Counterparts checked against Cliopatria geometry: the 260 loss is 184 of 188 cells in the Indo-Sasanian shape; the 270 loss of 3,390 cells is 1,339 cells in the Western Satraps' 270 shape and the rest ownerless; the final shape is 1,029 of 1,141 cells in the Gupta shape of 347.

Unsettled:
- Rajasthan, Sindh and Gujarat are drawn as Eastern Kushan in 238-269; no page opened for this state mentions them, and the Western Satraps' Junagadh list (150) names Sindhu-Sauvira, Maru and Kukura; the Satrap dossier carries the discussion.
- Gandhara is split in Cliopatria between the Eastern Kushans (to 259) and the Indo-Sasanians (from 260), while the Kushano-Sasanian page gives it to the Sasanians by 225 or 240-270; the 238 shape may be too generous in Gandhara.
- Whether the Kushan rulers of the Punjab ended in 346, 350 (Kipunada) or only with the Kidarite conquest (c. 390-410) depends on whether Gupta suzerainty counts as the end of the state. The Gupta group should record the Eastern Kushans as vassals of Samudragupta (vassal_start with counterpart eastern-kushans); this dossier ends the state with Cliopatria's last year at confidence 1.
- The Allahabad pillar's Daivaputra-Shahi-Shahanushahi has several readings (Kushans, Kushans and Sasanians, Shapur II, one ruler possibly Kidara I).
- The Nagas of Padmavati page dates the Nagas to the early 3rd century (Bhima-naga c. 210-230, Bhava-naga c. 310-335 on Trivedi's estimate) and ends them with Samudragupta in the mid-4th century, but finds 'no concrete evidence' that they defeated the Kushans; the Nagas of Vindhyatabi are not on any page opened. Neither has a dossier in this batch.

Counterparts needing dossiers: the Nagas of Padmavati (Pawaya near Gwalior, early 3rd century to the mid-4th, Kushan Empire page infobox successor and Gupta predecessor) and the Nagas of Vindhyatabi, suggested to the group's additions batch.
